inline.s: The characteristics of the world are ever-abiding.” Just as the Zhao Lun says:

The whirlwind levels the peaks and is ever still; the rivers rush on together yet do not flow; the dust of the wild horse flutters yet does not move; the sun and moon traverse the heavens yet do not revolve.

” (Translation: The fierce wind topples the mountains and is ever still; the rivers race on together yet do not flow; the dust is blown about yet does not move; the sun and moon pass across the sky yet neither rises nor sinks.)

The phrases in the passage, “the whirlwind levels the peaks,” “the rivers rush on together,” “the dust of the wild horse flutters,” “the sun and moon traverse the heavens,” describe the phenomenal marks (the marks of the world)

. Yet, seen in light of the real character of all dharmas, there are no whirlwind, no rivers, no wild horse, and no sun and moon at all (fundamentally nothing exists); how then could there be any leveling of peaks, rushing together, fluttering, or traversing the heavens? Therefore it is said: ever still, not flowing, not moving, not revolving. (For details see
The Real Character of All Dharmas
The Heart Sutra says:
“The empty character of all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
(For the annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra

[Whirlwind] Also called pila (vairambha), translated as “great fierce wind.” This is the great fierce wind that arises at the time of the world-ending catastrophe. [World-ending catastrophe] The three catastrophes of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three catastrophes sweep away the entire world. [The whirlwind levels the peaks] At the time of the world-ending catastrophe, the great fierce wind topples Mount Sumeru.

[Wild horse] A metaphor for dust. When spring arrives and the yang energy stirs, looking off toward the dust that rises among lakes and wilds resembles galloping horses, and so it is called “the wild horse.”

blocks.text: 7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole

inline.s: [7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole. This means that when one is at work on the practice, regarding the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner body and the outer worlds, all dharmas whatsoever â€” all are the very substance of the true mind, serene and still, void and bright, without so much as a hairsbreadth of difference; the great chiliocosm and the worlds of dust are beaten into one whole; where could any deluded mind be found? Thus the Master Zhao said: “Heaven and earth share the same root with me, and the myriad things are one body with me.” This is the work, practiced within and without as a single whole, of extinguishing delusion.]

7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole (inner and outer all become one body). When one is at work on the practice, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner body and mind and the outer worlds, all dharmas whatsoever â€” all are the very substance of the true mind, serene and still, void and bright, without so much as a hairsbreadth of difference. The great chiliocosm and all the worlds of dust are beaten into one whole; where could any deluded mind be found? Thus the great Master Sengzhao said: “Heaven and earth share the same root with me, and the myriad things are one body with me.” This is the work, practiced within and without as a single whole, of extinguishing delusion.

[World of things] The world of physical objects; this is a general term for the mountains, rivers, and great earth, houses, and all manner of implements and articles of use. It has the same meaning as the “world of material things.” [Chiliocosm of worlds] Great chiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [Chiliocosm] A thousand small worlds make one “small chiliocosm”; a thousand small chiliocosms make one “medium chiliocosm”; a thousand medium chiliocosms make one “great chiliocosm.” Because there are multiples of three thousands within it, the great chiliocosm is also called the “three-thousand-great-thousand world.”

blocks.text: 8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function

inline.s: [8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function. This means that when one is at work on the practice, one takes all dharmas whatsoever â€” inner and outer, body and mind, the worlds, and all actions and doings â€” and contemplates them all as the wondrous functioning of the true mind. The moment any thought arises it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since everything is the wondrous function, where can the deluded mind settle? Thus Yongjia said: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; this illusory empty body is precisely the Dharma-body.” The Song of the Twelve Hours of the Elder Zhigong says: “At the hour of dawn, the mad machine lies hidden in the Dao-body; whether sitting or lying, one knows not that this is the Way, but only bustles about toilsomely in suffering.” This is the work, practiced within and without as complete function, of stilling delusion.]

8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function. When one is at work on the practice, one takes all dharmas whatsoever â€” inner and outer, body and mind, the worlds, and all actions and doings â€” and contemplates them all as the wondrous function of the true mind. The moment any thought arises it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since everything is the wondrous function of the true mind, where can the deluded mind settle? Thus Yongjia s Certificate of the Way says: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; this illusory empty body is precisely the Dharma-body.” The Song of the Twelve Hours of the Elder Baozhi says: “At the hour of dawn, the mad machine lies hidden in the Dao-body; whether sitting or lying, one knows not that this is the Way, but only bustles about toilsomely in suffering.” This is the work, practiced within and without as complete function, of stilling delusion.
[Dawn] The early morning. [Yin] The yin hour (from three to five in the early morning). [Dawn, yin] This is the time when a cultivator of the Way rises.

[9. Substance and Function as One. This means that when one is at work on the practice, although one has silently merged with the true substance, a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a bright awareness â€” this is substance that is function; and within the bright awareness there is hidden emptiness and stillness â€” this is function that is substance. Thus Yongjia said: “What is mindful and still is right; what is mindful and deluded is wrong; what is still and mindful is right; what is indifferent and still is wrong.” Since within stillness there is no room for indifference, and within mindfulness no room for idle thinking, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work, in which substance and function are one, of extinguishing delusion.]

9. Substance and Function as One. When one is at work on the practice, although one has quietly merged with the true substance, a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a bright awareness â€” this is substance that is function; and within the bright awareness there is hidden emptiness and stillness â€” this is function that is substance. Thus the great Master Yongjia said: “To be mindful and yet still is right; to be mindful and yet deluded is wrong; to be still and yet mindful is right; to be indifferent and still is wrong.” Since within stillness there is no room for indifference, and within mindfulness no room for idle thinking, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work, in which substance and function are one, of extinguishing delusion.
[Mindful (
xing xing
)] Clear and alert in spirit. [Indifferent] Dull and sunk.

[10. Transcending Substance and Function. This means that when one is at work on the practice, one does not distinguish inner and outer, nor discern east, west, south, and north, but takes the four quarters and eight directions as a single great gate of liberation. Round and perfect, substance and function undivided, not the slightest leaking-through, the whole body beaten into one â€” where can any delusion arise? The ancients said: “The whole body has no crack or seam; above and below it is perfectly round.” This is the work, transcending substance and function, of extinguishing delusion.]

10. Transcending Substance and Function. When one is at work on the practice, one does not distinguish inner and outer, nor discern east, west, south, and north, but takes the four quarters and eight directions as a single great gate of liberation. Round and perfect, substance and function undivided, not a hair of leaking-through, the whole body beaten into one â€” where can the deluded mind arise? The ancients said: “The whole body has no crack or seam; above and below it is perfectly round.” This is the work, transcending substance and function, of extinguishing delusion.
[Crack or seam (
xia
)] A gap or fissure. [Very (
te
)] Too; exceedingly. [Perfectly round (
luan
)] Round in appearance; a reference to the full moon.

[Of the above ten methods of practicing, one need not use all of them. If but one method is brought to accomplishment, the delusion is extinguished of itself and the true mind appears. According to one s capacity and past habits, whichever method one has affinity with, practice that one. These practices are the work of no-effort, not an effort performed with a deliberate mind. This method of resting the deluded mind is the most essential, and therefore it has been spoken of at length; do not think it
(is)
prolix.]

Of the above ten methods of practicing, one need not use all of them. If only one method is brought to accomplishment, the delusion is extinguished of itself and the true mind appears. Therefore, following one s own capacity and past habits, whichever method one has had affinity with, adopt that method. These ten practices are the work of no-effort, not the effort of a deliberate mind. Since this method of resting delusion is the most essential, it has been spoken of at length; please do not feel it tedious.

blocks.text: 8. The Four Postures of the True Mind

inline.s: [The four postures] An abbreviation for the four deportments. [The four deportments] These are the rules that monks and nuns must observe, that is, being careful in the daily movements of daily life so as to maintain composure and dignity. The four deportments are: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. One should walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, and lie like a bow.

[Someone asks: In what was said before about stilling delusion â€” is it only by sitting in meditation that one practices, or does it also extend to walking, standing, and lying down? The answer: The sutras and treatises speak mostly of practicing by sitting, because sitting makes success easy; but when one has practiced for long and gradually become proficient, one may also practice in walking, standing, and lying down.]

The questioner asks: In what was said before about stilling delusion â€” is it only by sitting in meditation that one practices, or can one also practice while walking, standing, and lying down? The answer: The sutras and treatises speak mostly of practicing by sitting, because sitting makes success easy; when one has sat in meditation for long and gradually become proficient, one may then also practice in walking, standing, and lying down.

[The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “If one cultivates calm-abiding, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with right thought, not relying on the breath, not relying on forms and colors, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; all thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal itself is also cast away. Because all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought does not arise, thought after thought does not cease. Nor may one, after letting the mind go out to grasp an external realm, come to remove the mind by means of the mind. If the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. This right thought â€” know that it is mind-only, without any external realm; and this very mind likewise has no self-characteristic, for thought after thought is unobtainable.]

The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “If one cultivates calm-abiding, one should dwell in a quiet place and sit upright with right thought, not relying on the breath (not regulating the breath), not relying on forms and colors, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, and wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; all thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal is also cast away. This is because all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought does not arise, thought after thought does not cease. Nor may one let the mind go out to grasp an external realm and only then come to remove the mind by means of the mind. If the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. As to this right thought â€” know that all is mind-only, without any external realm, and this very mind also has no self-characteristic, because thought after thought is unobtainable.

[Cultivating calm-abiding] Doing the work of stilling deluded thoughts. [Seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing] A general term for the consciousness touching the external realm. The function of the eye-consciousness is “seeing,” of the ear-consciousness “hearing,” of the nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses “sensing,” and of the mental (sixth) consciousness “knowing.” [All thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal itself is cast away] “All thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise” is the work of bringing ten thousand thoughts to one. “Also casting away the thought of removal” is the work of bringing the one to nothing. [Nor may one, after letting the mind go out to grasp an external realm, come to remove the mind by means of the mind] Because to “remove the mind by means of the mind” in this way is to remove delusion with delusion, and to be swept along by delusion. This is the particular point to be careful of when doing the work of calm-abiding.

[If one rises from sitting and goes, comes, advances, and stops, doing whatever one does, at all times one should constantly bear in mind the skillful means and contemplate in accord with it. Practicing long and becoming proficient, the mind is able to abide. Because the mind abides, it gradually becomes sharp and keen, and following along it enters the samadhi of suchness, deeply subdues the afflictions, faith increases, and one quickly accomplishes the non-retrogressive. Only those who are doubtful, who do not believe and slander, those with heavy karmic obstructions, and the arrogant and indolent, are excepted. People such as these cannot enter it.” According to this, then the four deportments are all included.]

If one rises from the seat and goes out, comes in, advances, and stops, doing whatever one does, at all times one should use skillful means to contemplate according to conditions; if the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. Practicing long in this way and becoming proficient, deluded thoughts no longer arise (the mind is able to abide). Because deluded thoughts no longer arise (because the mind abides), the power of concentration gradually becomes ever more sharp and keen, and following along it enters the samadhi of suchness, deeply subduing the afflictions, faith increases, and one quickly accomplishes the non-retrogressive. Only those who are doubtful, who do not believe and slander, those with heavy karmic obstructions, and the arrogant and indolent are excepted. The samadhi of suchness cannot be entered by people such as these.” Based on this passage of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, it can be seen that the practice of stilling delusion in the true mind can be carried out in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “First rely on the Tathagata s practice of serenity, hold fast to the precepts, settle the assembly of disciples, and sit at ease in a quiet room.” This is the initial stage of practice. Yongjia said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the body is at ease.” According to this, the four deportments are likewise included.]

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “(Those who seek the Tathagata s pure and perfect enlightened mind should be of right thought and far from all illusions.) First one should cultivate calm-abiding (first rely on the Tathagata s practice of serenity), and for this one must hold fast to the precepts and settle the assembly of disciples, then sit at ease in a quiet room to practice.” This speaks of the initial stage of cultivating calm-abiding, which requires sitting in meditation. The great Master Yongjia said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the body is at ease.” Based on this passage of instruction, it can be seen that the practice of stilling delusion in the true mind can be carried out in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[Serenity (shamatha)] Translated into Chinese as “calm-abiding.” [Settle the assembly of disciples] To live in harmony with one s disciples and the great assembly. [Sit at ease] To sit silently and still.

[Summing up the merit of the practice: if while sitting one cannot still the mind, how much less can walking, standing, and lying down enter the Way? But for one who has used the practice to proficiency, though a thousand sages came they would not be startled into rising, though all manner of demons and heretics swarmed about he would not look back; how then could one be unable to practice in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down? It is like one who harbors hatred toward another: even while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, eating and drinking, in all actions, at all times he cannot forget it; and the one who loves another is likewise. Now hatred and love are matters of the concrete mind, and they can still be contained in the walking, standing, sitting, and lying down of the concrete mind; but the practice now is a matter of the no-mind. What doubt can there be that it would not constantly appear in the four deportments? I fear only that one will not believe and will not do it. If one only does it and believes it, then the Way within the deportments will surely not be lost.]

In sum, if in sitting still one cannot yet still the mind, how much less can one enter the Way while walking, standing, and lying down. But for one whose practice of stilling delusion in the true mind is used to proficiency, though a thousand sages came they would not startle him into rising, though all manner of demons and demons of every sort beset him, he would pay them no heed; how could it be that he cannot do the practice in walking, standing, and lying down? For example, if someone hates another, even while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, eating and drinking, and in all his doings, at all times he cannot forget it; and one who delights in another is likewise. Moreover hatred and love are matters of the concrete mind, and they can find room within the concrete mind in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The present practice, though, is a matter of the no-mind; what need is there to doubt that the practice could not constantly appear before one in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down? I only fear that one will not believe and not do it. If one believes and does it, then the practice of stilling delusion within walking, standing, sitting, and lying down will surely not be lost.
